jokes.text: He's the stupid garbage head doodoo face.
jokes.setup: Ben asks if Leslie is going to be civil when facing her nemesis Ron Swanson, noting she forbade anyone from saying his name because it fills her with rage.
jokes.punchline: Leslie insists she's 'perfectly civil' and then immediately calls Ron 'the stupid garbage head doodoo face' — a childish insult delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures Leslie Knope's character: her passionate, slightly unhinged intensity expressed through absurdly childish language. The setup ('are you gonna be civil?') + immediate ironic pivot ('I'm perfectly civil') + the kindergarten-level insult lands hard. The specificity of 'doodoo face' feels exactly right for Leslie — she's too earnest for actual profanity. Strong character integration; no one else on TV delivers this kind of line.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm perfectly civil when dealing with my nemesis.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Unlike some people, I don't resort to childish name-calling. Unlike you, bird-brain.

jokes.text: I'm gonna work until I'm 100 and then cut back to four days a week. Oh, God. I'm already so bored thinking about that one day off. Maybe I'll go to law school or something.
jokes.setup: Leslie is excited about the land deal being her crowning achievement and muses about retiring.
jokes.punchline: The concept of 'retiring' immediately spirals — she'd cut back to four days at 100, is bored imagining one day off, and would fill it with law school. The joke escalates in three beats.
jokes.explanation: A three-beat escalating joke that's deeply character-specific — only Leslie Knope would be bored by the idea of a day off at age 100. The rhythm is excellent: retirement → four days at 100 → bored by one day off → law school. Each beat tops the last. High character integration and strong structure make this one of the episode's craft highlights.

jokes.text: You're looking very Ron-like. / You have your same hair. / No, I don't! I have bangs now! / I've never known what bangs are, and I don't intend to learn!
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ron see each other for the first time after their falling out. Leslie tries to make a cutting remark about Ron's appearance.
jokes.punchline: Ron fires back that Leslie has 'the same hair,' Leslie insists she has bangs, and Ron delivers the perfectly Ron line: 'I've never known what bangs are, and I don't intend to learn.'
jokes.explanation: Ron's line is exceptional character comedy. His principled ignorance of trivial things (hair terminology) weaponized as a comeback is quintessential Ron Swanson. 'I don't intend to learn' is the perfect button — it's not just that he doesn't know, he's made a conscious decision to remain ignorant. Highly quotable. Economy is near-perfect. This is the episode's best standalone joke and earns its high score.

dialogue.speaker: Trevor
dialogue.line: You said, 'I would trade every tree in this country for a pile of cash.'

dialogue.speaker: Jessica
dialogue.line: Yeah, and I stand by that.

jokes.text: It's called Very Good Building and Development Company. I wanted to convey the quality of our work without seeming flashy.
jokes.setup: Ron explains he left Parks to run his own private sector company.
jokes.punchline: The company is called 'Very Good Building and Development Company' — deliberately plain, and Ron's earnest explanation that it conveys quality without flashiness is peak Ron logic.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly encapsulates Ron's philosophy: reject all pretension, name things accurately and plainly, and be proud of it. The joke has two layers — the absurdly literal name, and Ron's complete sincerity that this is the optimal branding strategy. Only Ron Swanson would name a company 'Very Good Building and Development Company.' Strong economy, maximum character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Retirement? I don't understand that word. Is that a type of government position? Because if it is, I'm already doing it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've already planned out my funeral agenda. It's a 47-point presentation with color-coded tabs.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Even my tombstone is going to have a five-year strategic plan carved into it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: My idea of relaxation is reorganizing my binders by both chronological order AND subject matter.

jokes.text: Oh, my gosh. It's perfect. The trees and rocks and the sky. Yes. The land has good sky.
jokes.setup: The Gryzzl rep explains they want to build their campus on the Newport land.
jokes.punchline: His reason for loving the land is 'trees and rocks and the sky' — ending with the non-observation 'the land has good sky,' delivered with total earnestness.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the vacuous specificity: listing sky as a unique selling point of land is delightfully idiotic. It satirizes tech-bro speak — enthusiastic about everything without saying anything. 'The land has good sky' is a quietly excellent non-sequitur.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Hello, Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Hey, Ron. So, um... how have you been? It's been a while since we've, you know, worked together and stuff.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We had that whole thing, remember? Where we were... together? But not in a weird way. Well, it was a little weird.

jokes.text: This guy, he's so far out. So normcore.
jokes.setup: The Gryzzl employee is watching Ron Swanson — a man who is literally the opposite of a tech trendster.
jokes.punchline: Calling Ron 'normcore' (a real micro-trend term meaning deliberately unstylish) as a compliment, when Ron would have absolutely zero awareness or interest in the concept.
jokes.explanation: The irony is rich — Ron would loathe being trendy, yet the trendiest people find him trendy for being so un-trendy. Solid satirical observation about tech culture appropriating authenticity, but the joke requires the audience to know what 'normcore' means.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So I'm thinking about getting bangs. What do you think?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't know anything about bangs, and I don't want to learn.

jokes.text: Leslie! I couldn't find that file you wanted, but I did find a file called Bird Census 1980. And it's empty. Get out of here, Ed! I fired you. Right. If anybody wants to hang, I will be at Subway.
jokes.setup: In the middle of Leslie's intense showdown speech about having 1,200 staff and creative geniuses, a bumbling subordinate interrupts.
jokes.punchline: Ed found nothing useful, found an empty file about birds, gets fired (again, apparently), and his response to being fired is to announce he'll be at Subway. The perfectly timed deflation of Leslie's bravado.
jokes.explanation: Classic comedic timing — Leslie just boasted about her 1,200 creative geniuses, then Ed shows up immediately to undercut her. The detail that the bird census file is empty is absurdly specific. 'I will be at Subway' as a post-firing plan is perfectly pathetic and oddly specific. The kicker 'He's very stupid' in talking head is the button. Strong structure (boast → immediate deflation) and good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm starting a woodworking company. I'm going to call it Ron Swanson Woodworking.

jokes.text: He's very stupid. [Talking head]
jokes.setup: Ed announces he'll be at Subway after being fired.
jokes.punchline: Cut to Leslie in a talking head simply stating 'He's very stupid.' The dry, matter-of-fact assessment after the chaos is the button.
jokes.explanation: The brevity is the joke. After everything Ed just did, the most devastating response is total understatement. Good economy, good structure as a button/callback to the prior scene.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: This land is absolutely magnificent! The views are spectacular, the air is crisp and clean, and the sky... the sky is so blue!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Yes, the sky is indeed blue.

jokes.text: Babe, I just dropped off Leslie's triplets with her mom. All three of 'em. Nailed it.
jokes.setup: Ben casually mentions dropping off Leslie's triplets.
jokes.punchline: 'All three of 'em. Nailed it.' — the self-congratulation for accomplishing the bare minimum (returning all three children) implies this was a harder task than it sounds.
jokes.explanation: The implied joke is that 'all three of 'em' suggests a non-trivial possibility of losing one, and 'Nailed it' is hilariously low-bar self-praise. Quick, clean, and character-appropriate for new-dad Ben.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: Ron is like a blockchain-enabled, cloud-native, synergistic disruptor who's completely off the grid and doesn't know what email is.

jokes.text: Welcome back to the Johnny Karate Super Awesome Musical Explosion Show.
jokes.setup: Andy mentions he has his own TV show.
jokes.punchline: The show is called 'Johnny Karate Super Awesome Musical Explosion Show' — an absurdly maximalist title that is absolutely perfect for Andy.
jokes.explanation: The show name is peak Andy Dwyer — every word is maximum enthusiasm with no filter or restraint. 'Super Awesome Musical Explosion' stacks superlatives incoherently. Only Andy would name a children's show this way and it's completely believable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Remember when you said you'd never work with me again?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I said that in 1997. It's now 2009. I clearly changed my mind.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But you were so adamant about it.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: People evolve, Leslie. Even me.

jokes.text: I'm Mailman Barry. Morning, Barry. I have something for you. Andy, no. Ninjas attack! Andy. No. That's my crotch. Okay, guys. Three more kicks apiece.
jokes.setup: A mailman comes to the set of Andy's children's TV show apparently for a wholesome segment.
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately orders ninjas to attack him, someone (likely an adult crew member) gets kicked in the crotch, and Andy's resolution is 'Three more kicks apiece' — completely normalizing crotch violence on a children's show.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Andy's children's show is chaotic and possibly dangerous — a consistent characterization. 'That's my crotch' lands as a great unexpected reaction beat, and 'Three more kicks apiece' as a solution is wonderful: Andy isn't stopping the kicks, just making it equal opportunity.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have a large, dedicated staff working on this initiative.

dialogue.speaker: Ed
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm Ed. Leslie fired me three days ago.

jokes.text: Leslie, I have always liked you. Yeah, no, you haven't though.
jokes.setup: Jessica says she's always liked Leslie as she's about to decline to give a discount.
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately and flatly corrects her — 'Yeah, no, you haven't though' — which is both accurate and hilariously blunt.
jokes.explanation: The flat truth-telling is the joke. Leslie doesn't play along with the social nicety even for strategic purposes — she just corrects the record. The 'yeah, no' construction is characteristically mid-American and real. Good economy, good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ed, you're fired.

dialogue.speaker: Ed
dialogue.line: Oh, okay. Well, hey everyone, want to grab lunch at Subway later?

jokes.text: Leslie doesn't pay for my lifestyle. Money does. So, between money and Leslie... You see the bind that I'm in.
jokes.setup: Jessica says she likes Leslie but also likes money, which pays for her lifestyle.
jokes.punchline: Framing Leslie vs. money as a genuine dilemma — 'You see the bind that I'm in' — delivered without irony. Jessica is completely serious that this is a hard choice.
jokes.explanation: Jessica's oblivious honesty is her entire character — she's not cruel, just transparently materialistic. The formal 'bind' framing for such a shallow conflict is the joke. Character-specific and well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ed is insane. Like, clinically. We looked into it.

jokes.text: Well, thank you, Jessica. You did and said exactly what I thought you were gonna do and say. And that's oddly comforting.
jokes.setup: Jessica has just politely declined to give any discount on her land.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response is to sincerely thank Jessica for being predictably unhelpful, finding comfort in the predictability itself.
jokes.explanation: A nicely inverted response — Leslie takes genuine comfort in a disappointing outcome because at least it was predictable. Reveals her planner personality in an amusing way. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I counted to ten today. Without using my fingers.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm not gonna lie, I'm feeling pretty smart right now.

jokes.text: Who is Tom Haverford? He's a mentor, a lover, a hero. But who is my hero? Simple. It's me five years from now.
jokes.setup: A reporter or interviewer asks Tom to describe himself for a profile.
jokes.punchline: Tom's hero is himself — but specifically future himself, five years from now. The triple self-description (mentor, lover, hero) followed by the revelation that HE is asking who HIS hero is, answered by 'me, five years from now,' is layered narcissism.
jokes.explanation: This joke has real craft. The setup mimics the format of inspirational profiles ('Who is your hero?'), then subverts it with maximum Tom-ness. 'Mentor, a lover, a hero' as self-description is already good, but 'me five years from now' is the perfect button — it's both deeply narcissistic AND kind of self-motivating in a Tom way. Highly quotable, strong character integration, well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: The name of my show is 'Andy's Awesome Adventure Time Fun Extravaganza Explosion.'

jokes.text: I own Pawnee's hottest restaurant, two fast casual eateries, and the Tommy Chopper. We serve chopped salads out of a decommissioned military helicopter. I'm a mogul now!
jokes.setup: Tom is listing his business accomplishments for a magazine profile.
jokes.punchline: The Tommy Chopper — serving chopped salads from a decommissioned military helicopter — is the escalating absurd detail that caps the list, followed by the triumphant 'I'm a mogul now!'
jokes.explanation: The Tommy Chopper is an inspired piece of absurdism that feels completely earned for Tom — it's over-the-top, has a pun in the name (chopper/chopped salads), and the military surplus detail makes it weirder and better. 'I'm a mogul now!' is the perfect capping declaration. High originality.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Kick me in the crotch again!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What? No.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Come on, just one more time. It felt amazing!

jokes.text: Ben Wyatt! City Manager of Pawnee. The Chamber of Commerce asked me to introduce him at a very fancy black tie gala tonight. One of the many area bigwigs who comes to me for life advice, fashion tips... You get it.
jokes.setup: Tom mentions Ben in his talking head.
jokes.punchline: Ben Wyatt — a notoriously khaki-and-fleece-wearing accountant-type — coming to Tom for 'fashion tips' is the ironic joke, enhanced by Tom's breezy 'You get it.'
jokes.explanation: Competent character comedy playing on known dynamics — Ben as fashion disaster, Tom as self-appointed style guru. Works for fans but not especially inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This land is worth millions of dollars!

dialogue.speaker: Jessica
dialogue.line: I know. I'm very valuable.

jokes.text: So, for the introduction, I'd love it if you could just keep it brief. Like stick to my fiscal accomplishments. Wanna wake me up when you're done boring us to death, am I right, Janet? Write down that I'm funny.
jokes.setup: Ben asks Tom to keep the introduction brief and focused on fiscal accomplishments.
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately mocks Ben's request as boring, turns to a presumably nonexistent or confused Janet, then turns the moment into self-promotion by instructing the profiler to 'write down that I'm funny.'
jokes.explanation: 'Write down that I'm funny' is a great button — the joke being that Tom needs to instruct people to record his humor rather than it being self-evident. The 'Janet' pivot also works as a comedian doing a bit mid-conversation.

dialogue.speaker: Jessica
dialogue.line: We're best friends!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, we're not.

jokes.text: Constantly. [Tom asks 'When's Tommy ever let you down?']
jokes.setup: Tom asks rhetorically 'When's Tommy ever let you down?' expecting Ben to play along.
jokes.punchline: Ben answers without hesitation: 'Constantly.' Complete deadpan, no elaboration.
jokes.explanation: The entire joke is in one word delivered at precisely the right moment. Economy is flawless — there is literally no better way to make this joke. Ben's long history of being let down by Tom makes it earned rather than cheap. The absolute best one-word comebacks score high on economy.

dialogue.line: Treating money vs. doing good as equally weighted options

jokes.text: It's my biggest project since Ice Town, so it really means a lot that I'm being recognized as a city leader instead of being yelled at and pelted with things.
jokes.setup: Ben is talking about being honored at the gala for organizing the Bicentennial Celebration.
jokes.punchline: Revealing that his baseline for 'city leader' was previously being 'yelled at and pelted with things' — a reference to the Ice Town disaster that defined his character.
jokes.explanation: Richly character-specific — Ben's greatest shame (Ice Town) is woven in naturally, and 'pelted with things' is a wonderfully specific and vivid image. The low bar of 'not being pelted' as a success metric is both funny and a little sad. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.line: How do you spell your name?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: T-O-M. But it's pronounced 'Thomas.' I'm a complex man with a lot of layers, like an onion. Or a parfait.

jokes.text: Wait. You don't think this is all an elaborate setup to pelt me with things, do you?
jokes.setup: Ben just mentioned being pelted at Ice Town; now he's about to receive an honor.
jokes.punchline: Ben's trauma is so deep he genuinely wonders if the gala honoring him is actually an elaborate pelt-trap.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback within the same beat — the joke intensifies. Ben's paranoia about being pelted reveals genuine PTSD about Ice Town. 'Elaborate setup to pelt me with things' is a great specific phrasing.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I've started three successful businesses. First, there was my entertainment company, then my clothing line, and now... my helicopter salad restaurant.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You order a salad, and while you're eating it, a helicopter flies over your table and blows all the lettuce around. It's farm-to-table freshness meets aerospace innovation.

jokes.text: The new Jason Bourne movie is supposed to be pretty funny.
jokes.setup: Andy and April are planning their week like 'old people' and Andy suggests a movie night.
jokes.punchline: Andy describes the new Jason Bourne movie as 'supposed to be pretty funny' — a spy action thriller being called 'pretty funny' reveals Andy's total obliviousness to genre, paid off later in the episode when the Jason Bourne quote comes up.
jokes.explanation: A sleeper joke that pays off later. Andy calling an action movie 'pretty funny' is in-character for his obliviousness. Gets better on rewatch when you notice Leslie later quotes Jason Bourne.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ben is like a human calculator. Except calculators are useful and people actually like them.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Can we get that on record?

jokes.text: Andy, we're planning our whole week, like old people!
jokes.setup: Andy and April have been discussing the slow cooker, brisket, production meetings, dinner plans, and movies — a normal adult week.
jokes.punchline: April's horror at recognizing they've become responsible planners, framed as 'like old people.'
jokes.explanation: Relatable observational comedy about growing up filtered through April and Andy's specific horror at normalcy. The concept isn't highly original but it's well-executed through these characters.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm really honored to be here. Though I have to say, it's a little triggering given my past failures.

jokes.text: We used to eat cereal out of Frisbees because we didn't have any bowls. You once broke a rib trying to wrestle one of those inflatable floppy guys at a car dealership. I won.
jokes.setup: April and Andy bemoan becoming boring adults, listing evidence of their former spontaneity.
jokes.punchline: Andy broke a rib wrestling an inflatable tube-man at a car dealership — and his immediate response to April mentioning this is 'I won,' delivered with complete sincerity and pride.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's comic highlight alongside joke #3. Two layers: the escalating absurdism of the activities (Frisbee bowls → broken rib vs. tube man), and then Andy's 'I won' — delivered as though winning a wrestling match against an inflatable promotional figure is a genuine accomplishment he's proud of. The specificity ('inflatable floppy guys at a car dealership') is perfect. 'I won' is the best two-word punchline in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm telling you, it could happen again. I've seen it happen. I've *lived* it. You don't just come back from being pelted with something and act like it's not a constant threat.

jokes.text: We have a bank account! / That's it. We've held out as long as we could, but it finally happened. We're boring. We're boring people who bore each other by being boring.
jokes.setup: The list of responsible adult behaviors culminates in the horror of having a bank account.
jokes.punchline: April's declaration that they are boring is delivered like a terminal diagnosis, and 'boring people who bore each other by being boring' is the beautifully tautological verbal spiral.
jokes.explanation: The triple repetition of 'boring' is a nice rhetorical escalation — it spirals and collapses on itself comedically. April's deadpan delivery of an existential crisis about adulthood is well-played.

jokes.text: I only have $2 million in the discretionary fund, and I've already used some of it to make Thomas Jefferson sexier in those Mount Rushmore promotions. Which, by the way, attendance has been up. That's not a coincidence.
jokes.setup: Leslie needs $90 million to buy the land and is going through her available funds.
jokes.punchline: She's already spent some of her discretionary budget sexying up Thomas Jefferson on Mount Rushmore promotions — and she's proud of the results.
jokes.explanation: Highly original comedic premise — using federal funds to make a founding father 'sexy' in promotional materials, and the attendance data confirming it worked. Leslie's matter-of-fact 'That's not a coincidence' is perfect conviction comedy. This detail is inventive and specific to Leslie's particular brand of passionate civic boosterism. One of the episode's best absurdist moments.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You once drove a car into a lake.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: And I got out alive! That's a win in my book.

jokes.text: That tuxedo makes you look like a sexy orchestra conductor. Here. Wave this pen around.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to focus Ben on the mission of fundraising at the gala.
jokes.punchline: She compliments his tuxedo by comparing him to a sexy orchestra conductor, then hands him a pen to wave around to complete the bit.
jokes.explanation: A small, pleasant joke — the pen-as-baton detail is a nice physical comedy add-on. Not especially memorable but delivers a light moment in an otherwise exposition-heavy scene.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We're using federal funds to sexualize Thomas Jefferson.

jokes.text: Ken Hotate! Great bolo tie. Is that new? Why, yes, it is. My son sells them on Etsy. He is a huge disappointment.
jokes.setup: Leslie admires Ken Hotate's bolo tie as a conversational opener.
jokes.punchline: Ken's explanation that his son sells them on Etsy is immediately followed by 'He is a huge disappointment' — a total non-sequitur shift in register that reveals Ken considers Etsy entrepreneurship beneath his son's potential.
jokes.explanation: The joke has perfect architecture: compliment → innocent explanation → devastating pivot. The specific disappointment of Etsy crafts being beneath Ken's Native American chief dignity is culturally specific to the character. 'He is a huge disappointment' with no elaboration is textbook economy. The pivot is sudden and surprising.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I may not have as much money as my opponents, but I have something they don't have: an almost delusional sense of optimism and a complete inability to accept defeat.

jokes.text: So you would like the Wamapoke people to pay the federal government millions of dollars to buy land that was stolen from us by the federal government? And we don't even get to keep the land?
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Ken to donate casino money to help the federal government buy the Newport Land for a national park.
jokes.punchline: Ken lays out the full absurdity of what Leslie is asking — essentially asking Native Americans to fund the government's purchase of their own stolen land, which they won't even own.
jokes.explanation: This joke does real work. It's both genuinely funny and pointed social commentary. The structure of restating Leslie's request as a logical sequence exposes the absurdity powerfully. Ken Hotate's deadpan delivery of historical injustice as an argument-ender is both dark and earned. The character's dignity in delivering this makes it land harder than if it were played for broader comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ken
dialogue.line: My son gave me this bolo tie.

dialogue.speaker: Ken
dialogue.line: He's not a good person.

jokes.text: Well, when you put it like that, I see the irony. So, are you in? No? What if I buy some of your disappointing son's bolo ties?
jokes.setup: Ken has just eloquently explained why Leslie's request is historically absurd.
jokes.punchline: Leslie acknowledges the irony for one second, then barrels ahead asking if he's in, and when met with a 'no,' immediately pivots to buying bolo ties — calling back Ken's son being a 'huge disappointment.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback that rewards the earlier setup. Leslie's rapid acknowledgment-and-pivot past the historical injustice is very Leslie — she heard it, processed it, and moved on in one breath. The bolo tie callback is perfectly timed. 'Damn it' from Ken after Leslie offers to buy bolo ties implies he's considering it, which is its own joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Ken, I need you to donate the land so we can turn it into a park.

dialogue.speaker: Ken
dialogue.line: You want me to give you my land so you can make a park out of it? Leslie, that's literally the opposite of what a businessman does.

jokes.text: Hey, check it out. I'm so crazy and spontaneous, I don't even need this sling anymore.
jokes.setup: Andy and April are trying to prove they're still spontaneous and fun at the gala.
jokes.punchline: Andy removes his arm sling as a demonstration of spontaneity and immediately injures himself again (implied by 'Did you hear that pop?').
jokes.explanation: Quick, physical, character-perfect. The irony that his attempt to prove spontaneity causes immediate re-injury is tight. 'Did you hear that pop?' is a great specific detail that implies a new injury without showing it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Look, I know things got off to a rocky start, but your son is a really great guy. I mean, sure, he made some questionable decisions, but who hasn't? I once tried to make a quilt out of dog hair. We all have our moments.

dialogue.speaker: Ken
dialogue.line: My son is disappointing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, yes, but—

dialogue.speaker: Ken
dialogue.line: No, I mean, he's a very disappointing person.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, but if it helps, I'm sure that's not entirely his fault. Parenting is really hard, and—

dialogue.speaker: Ken
dialogue.line: He gets it from his mother.

jokes.text: I dare you to eat this entire jug of olives. Done.
jokes.setup: Andy and April are looking for something spontaneous and weird to do at the fancy gala.
jokes.punchline: April's idea of a wild dare is eating a jug of olives; Andy accepts instantly and without hesitation.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'jug of olives' is right. It's not a bottle or a jar — a jug. April's dare is itself silly, and Andy's instantaneous acceptance is perfect Andy. Quick and clean.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna do something wild and spontaneous!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? What?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna eat this whole pizza without checking the nutritional information first!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Wow, living on the edge.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, hold on. I need to make sure I'm staying within my daily recommended sodium intake and get the macronutrient breakdown. Let me look this up real quick.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: And there it is.

jokes.text: What are you doing? / I'm gonna take a Zantac. All that salt will give me heartburn. / Oh, God. You ruined it.
jokes.setup: Andy begins eating the olive jug dare; April waits for wild spontaneity.
jokes.punchline: Andy stops to proactively take a Zantac for heartburn prevention — the most responsible, boring-adult move possible, which April identifies as ruining their attempt at spontaneity.
jokes.explanation: This is a gem. The setup is Andy attempting something wild, but the punchline is the Zantac — the most un-wild possible accessory to olive-eating. Andy preemptively managing his heartburn mid-dare is devastating. It perfectly executes the episode's theme (they've become responsible adults) through action rather than declaration. 'You ruined it' is the perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm rallying the old team back together. We're going to make a real difference in this town.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That sounds great, Leslie. I'm in... as long as there's a consulting fee for me.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What? I have a family to support. Actually, make it two consulting fees.

jokes.text: Should I still take the Zantac? Yeah, you always feel better when you do.
jokes.setup: April has declared that Andy taking Zantac 'ruined' their spontaneous moment.
jokes.punchline: Andy still asks if he should take it, and April immediately tells him yes because it genuinely helps — completely surrendering to responsible adulthood while pretending to resist it.
jokes.explanation: The button to the Zantac joke and somehow better than the setup. April's 'you always feel better when you do' is the complete capitulation — she's not mad at the Zantac, she's mad at what it represents. Their resignation and the loving practicality of 'you always feel better when you do' is both funny and quietly touching.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Look, I'm on Ron's side because Shia LaBeouf is designing the wedding dress.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. I hate us, let's go.
jokes.setup: Andy and April have fully surrendered to their responsible adult selves.
jokes.punchline: April's summation: 'I hate us' — delivered with total flat affect before immediately moving on.
jokes.explanation: 'I hate us' is a perfectly April line — self-loathing delivered as a dry statement of fact, then immediately moving on. Maximum economy. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: Well, it all started when I was born. My parents named me Garry with two r's, which is apparently very uncommon. Then in the second grade, a teacher started calling me Larry, and it just stuck. So for years, I've been going by Larry. But then I realized, you know, my real name is actually Jerry. So I decided to go back to Jerry. It's my real name.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: And you know what? I'm okay with it. Sure, nobody calls me by my real name. Sure, I've been called every name but my own. But that's life, isn't it? You just have to roll with the punches and keep smiling.

jokes.text: Oh, actually, Ron promised me I could build a restaurant on the new Gryzzl campus. So I'm kind of totally on Ron's side. / Okay, Tom's dead to me.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks her old team to join her in 'Defeat Ron' mission, expecting loyalty.
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately reveals he's switched sides for a restaurant deal, and Leslie's response — 'Tom's dead to me' — is immediate and total, no negotiation.
jokes.explanation: Effective misdirection — the 'hands in' team moment is subverted immediately. Tom's pragmatic betrayal (for restaurant space) and Leslie's over-the-top response ('dead to me') play well against each other. Character-appropriate on both sides.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Pawnee's not on the map. Except for this very specific and unflattering statistic.

jokes.text: Shia LaBeouf designed wedding dresses do not come cheap.
jokes.setup: Donna explains she needs the money from working with Ron for her upcoming wedding.
jokes.punchline: The specific detail that her wedding dress will be designed by Shia LaBeouf — an actor not known for fashion design — is the absurdist joke.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of Shia LaBeouf as wedding dress designer is perfect — it's not a joke about Shia LaBeouf being bad, it's a joke about Donna's specifically Donna-esque aspirations. It's an absurd status marker that somehow perfectly fits Donna's character. High originality for the unexpectedness of the celebrity choice.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This is Ben Wyatt, the man who literally lifted up this entire town with his bare hands and his brilliant mind.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And that's why I'm naming my new restaurant after him: Sweetums.

jokes.text: You know, they're trying to destroy us. There's three of them, it's insane, but they're great.
jokes.setup: Someone asks how Leslie and Ben's triplets are doing.
jokes.punchline: 'They're trying to destroy us' as a description of toddlers — stated with the exhaustion of a new parent — followed by the immediate pivot to 'but they're great.'
jokes.explanation: A familiar parenting joke ('kids are destroying me') elevated slightly by the specificity of triplets and Ben's deadpan delivery. Functional but not especially fresh.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not stealing your team, Leslie. I'm simply allocating resources more efficiently. These shrimp skewers need to be exactly 4.3 inches long for optimal cooking and structural integrity.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, that's insane. You're literally measuring shrimp.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Not measuring. Optimizing. There's a difference. Now if you'll excuse me, this one is 4.2 inches. Unacceptable.

jokes.text: Well, never fear, because Terry is here. Yes, I go by Terry now. Because there was a guy at National Parks. He was already named Larry, so they suggested I go by Terry. And then I said my real name is Gary, and they said, 'Who cares?' So, it's just a fun group.
jokes.setup: The running gag of this character's name being wrong continues — he spent the series being called Larry, his real name is Gary.
jokes.punchline: At his new job he was renamed Terry because there was already a Larry, and when he revealed his real name was Gary, the response was 'Who cares?' — the universe continuing to deny him his correct name. 'So, it's just a fun group' is the perfectly resigned button.
jokes.explanation: The most character-specific joke in the episode for Gary. The escalation of wrong names (Larry → Terry → 'who cares about Gary?') is perfectly structured. 'So, it's just a fun group' — his cheerful acceptance of being repeatedly misidentified — is heartbreaking and hilarious. This joke rewards seven seasons of the name gag with a perfect extension. High marks for character integration and earned humor.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm the best at staying humble. I'm humble as hell. Nobody's more humble than me. I'm like the LeBron James of humility.

jokes.text: Not long ago, this town was barely on the map. Unless you're talking about a map of the cities with the most obese pets.
jokes.setup: Tom begins a grandiose introduction speech at the gala.
jokes.punchline: The exception carved out for 'most obese pets' map is a perfect Pawnee-specific joke — the town's consistent characterization as deeply, specifically troubled.
jokes.explanation: Efficiently establishes Pawnee's absurd baseline with a specific, original detail. 'Obese pets' rather than just 'obese people' is a fresh angle on the Pawnee-dysfunction joke. Well-structured as a self-aware gala speech.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'd like to thank the Parks Department for this magnificent statue. It really captures the essence of... whatever this is supposed to be. The artist did an amazing job making it look exactly like someone who's never seen a human before tried to sculpt one from a description. It's truly a masterpiece of 'I have no idea what I'm doing.' I'm going to treasure this forever, or at least until I can figure out how to dispose of it without anyone noticing.

jokes.text: But then one great man came along and he lifted all of us up. / [Long pause, implication he'll name Ben] / And that man was me. Tom Haverford...
jokes.setup: Tom appears to be building toward introducing Ben as the great man who lifted Pawnee up.
jokes.punchline: The 'great man' is Tom himself. He's introducing himself mid-introduction of someone else.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection with good structural tension — the pause lets the audience expect Ben's name. Tom inserting himself as the subject is well-timed and character-perfect. Only Tom Haverford would do this.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron is like Voldemort. You don't say his name, you just point and people know who you mean.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not a dark wizard.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, but you're just as powerful and just as scary.

jokes.text: People come up to me, and they say things like, 'Tom, given all that you've accomplished, is it hard to stay humble?' And I say, 'Not for me. I'm pretty amazing at being humble.'
jokes.setup: Tom continues his self-aggrandizing speech at the gala.
jokes.punchline: Tom claims to be 'amazing at being humble' — a textbook self-undermining statement delivered without any awareness of the contradiction.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed ironic reversal — the classic 'I'm great at being humble' contradiction. Not highly original (this joke form exists) but executed well with Tom-specific flavor. The 'people come up to me' framing adds an extra layer of self-mythology.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Leslie fighting over cake is way crazier than us streaking.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, we're not getting cake?

jokes.text: Thank you. Thanks. And thank you to Tom for that moving tribute to you.
jokes.setup: Ben takes the podium after Tom's extended self-tribute introduction.
jokes.punchline: Ben thanks Tom for the 'moving tribute to you' — meaning Tom's tribute to himself rather than to Ben, delivered with perfectly dry delivery.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy, perfect timing. One sentence does it all — acknowledges what just happened, roasts Tom, and reveals Ben's quiet wit. 'Moving tribute to you' (Tom, not to Ben) is economical and sharp. This lands as a big laugh because it comes immediately after the longest possible setup.

dialogue.speaker: Jessica
dialogue.line: I love my new Gryzzl tablet so much!

dialogue.speaker: Gryzzl Tablet
dialogue.line: I know. I've been watching you sleep.

jokes.text: And thank you to the Boys and Girls Club for the incredibly life-like papier-mâché statue.
jokes.setup: Ben continues his acceptance speech, acknowledging the decorations.
jokes.punchline: There is apparently a papier-mâché statue of Ben at the event — which he thanks the Boys and Girls Club for, implying children made it — and it is described as 'incredibly life-like,' which implies it probably isn't.
jokes.explanation: A good visual gag inferred from dialogue — the statue exists and looks like Ben (apparently), made by children. The 'incredibly life-like' in Ben's deadpan implies either it's worryingly accurate or hilariously not. The Boys and Girls Club attribution makes it funnier — these are children.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I have to pay taxes, and my car insurance is due, and I need to schedule a dentist appointment.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Honestly, at this point, I'm ready to form a suicide pact with someone.

jokes.text: And thank you to the Boys and Girls Club for the incredibly life-like papier-mâché statue.
jokes.setup: Ben continues his acceptance remarks after the Tom speech
jokes.punchline: He thanks the Boys and Girls Club for a papier-mâché statue — implying it exists and is being passed off as impressive
jokes.explanation: A good visual-gag inference: there is presumably a lumpy papier-mâché statue on stage, and Ben thanks the children who made it with the same decorum as a professional sculpture. 'Incredibly life-like' is the dry lie that makes it work.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Where are we?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We're in the part of town that's only populated by raccoons and car batteries.

jokes.text: How about this? We shut off the lights, turn 'em back on. Everybody's fancy jewelry is missing. Meanwhile, you and I are already on a boat to the airport.
jokes.setup: Andy and April are scheming to do something spontaneous and wild at the gala.
jokes.punchline: Andy's plan is essentially a jewelry heist from the gala guests, followed by fleeing by boat to an airport — logistically absurd (boats to airports?) but Andy is completely serious.
jokes.explanation: Wonderfully specific absurdist plan — 'on a boat to the airport' is the detail that makes it. Andy has clearly thought about this. The escalation from 'something fun' to 'full jewelry heist' is quintessential Andy logic.

jokes.text: Let's put stink bombs in all the vents. Yes. Wait. No. I forgot. I got rid of all the stink bombs before I babysat Leslie's kids.
jokes.setup: Andy and April are generating increasingly wild plans.
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately embraces stink bombs, then remembers he responsibly disposed of his entire stink bomb collection before babysitting — revealing that (1) he owned a stink bomb collection, and (2) he was responsible enough to get rid of them for the kids.
jokes.explanation: Two jokes in one: Andy OWNED stink bombs (absurd), AND he responsibly got rid of them before babysitting (he IS growing up). The joke works on the comedy level and the character arc level simultaneously. 'Being responsible adults sucks butts' is the perfect button. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Realtor
dialogue.line: Well, the kitchen flows directly into the master bedroom, the bathroom is actually inside the living room, and the garage is on the second floor. But other than that, it's really just your standard layout.

jokes.text: Being responsible adults sucks butts.
jokes.setup: Andy has just revealed he got rid of his stink bombs to be a responsible babysitter.
jokes.punchline: 'Being responsible adults sucks butts' — quintessentially Andy vocabulary ('butts') applied to an adult emotion.
jokes.explanation: 'Sucks butts' as adult existential complaint is perfectly Andy — the vocabulary of a ten-year-old expressing a grown-up feeling. Maximum economy. Highly quotable because it perfectly encapsulates Andy's voice.

dialogue.speaker: Realtor
dialogue.line: It wasn't the factory but the asylum for the workers.

jokes.text: Butts. That's it. I'll streak across the stage. Yes. I love it. I'm gonna get naked. I'm gonna get up there. Everyone is gonna see my wiener. I mean, you've seen it. You know how dumb it looks.
jokes.setup: Andy hears himself say 'butts' and is immediately inspired to streak.
jokes.punchline: Andy's enthusiasm for public nudity is absolute, and the self-deprecating qualifier 'You know how dumb it looks' about his own anatomy is completely unexpected and wonderfully specific.
jokes.explanation: 'You know how dumb it looks' is the unexpected turn that makes this joke — Andy's self-assessment of his own anatomy as 'dumb-looking' delivered matter-of-factly to April is charmingly weird. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Trevor
dialogue.line: I'm proud to announce the opening of my new law firm: Batting Average, On-Base Percentage & Slugging Percentage.

jokes.text: I told you to never say that word to me! No one should ever say that word out loud. It's like 'Voldemort' or 'Ron.'
jokes.setup: Ron mentions Morningstar (the development project that caused their falling-out) during the argument.
jokes.punchline: Leslie compares 'Morningstar' to 'Voldemort' — a name too terrible to speak — and then appends 'or Ron' to the list, making Ron himself a word she can't say, returning to the opening bit.
jokes.explanation: The Voldemort comparison is solid; the callback to Ron's name being forbidden makes it a tight callback structure. The fact that 'Ron' himself becomes a Voldemort word is a clean callback to the episode's opening.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Who am I? I don't even know anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's from Jason Bourne.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Kevin James should play Jason Bourne.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, he shouldn't.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Kevin James as Jason Bourne.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Stop it.

jokes.text: You don't deserve that candle! Give me that candle! Let go! Let go! This candle's mine! No! Gimme this candle. You steal my team, I steal your candle! I stole nothing!
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ron's argument at the gala escalates beyond words.
jokes.punchline: They physically fight over a candle — a completely trivial object — with full sincerity, while other guests watch. The stakes (world-class argument) vs. the prize (one candle) is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The physical absurdism of two serious adults fighting over a gala candle channels the emotional stakes of their broken friendship into the most trivial possible outlet. 'You steal my team, I steal your candle' is Leslie's logic at its most unhinged. Good visual comedy even inferred from dialogue.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have declared war on the Sweetums factory, and I'm going to fight them with the only weapon I have: delicious, homemade cookies baked with love and fury.

jokes.text: It's okay. Everything's fine. Just wheel out the backup cake. / There's no backup cake. / Who doesn't bake a backup cake?
jokes.setup: Ben tries to manage the chaos of Leslie and Ron's candle fight during the gala.
jokes.punchline: Ben assumes there's a backup cake; the staff confirms there isn't; Ben's genuine outrage at the lack of contingency baking reveals his event-planner logic (always have a backup).
jokes.explanation: 'Who doesn't bake a backup cake?' is a great line — it's both absurd (backup cake isn't standard) and entirely reasonable in context (Leslie destroyed the main cake). Ben's calm catastrophe management is character-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm declaring war on you all. I'm going to destroy you.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I made war cookies.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, these have hearts in them.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know. I can't fully commit to being mean.

jokes.text: They're still gonna serve that cake, right?
jokes.setup: The entire gala has descended into chaos with the candle fight and destroyed cake.
jokes.punchline: Andy's only concern through all of this is whether the cake will still be served.
jokes.explanation: Andy's single-minded food focus cutting through the drama is perfect. Maximum economy — one line does it all. The audience knows Andy only cares about the cake and it lands exactly as expected but satisfyingly.

jokes.text: Okay. Well, that seals it. Even Leslie is crazier than we are.
jokes.setup: Andy and April have been despairing about being boring; they've just watched Leslie and Ron fight over a candle and destroy the gala cake.
jokes.punchline: April uses Leslie's candle meltdown as evidence that they're not the craziest people in the room — reframing their 'boring' problem through Leslie's chaos.
jokes.explanation: A good structural button on the Andy/April arc — Leslie's chaos resolves their worry about being boring. 'Even Leslie' is the right framing. Efficient and satisfying.

jokes.text: I love your skin. Give me your skin. Oh! There are still a couple bugs with the AI software. But maybe just turn it off before you go to sleep.
jokes.setup: The Gryzzl rep gives Jessica a prototype tablet as a gift.
jokes.punchline: The tablet's AI says 'I love your skin. Give me your skin.' — an unsettling AI request — and the rep's response is a casual 'couple bugs, just turn it off before bed,' treating a skin-harvesting AI as a minor software glitch.
jokes.explanation: Inspired absurdist dark comedy about AI and tech company recklessness. 'Give me your skin' is a wonderfully disturbing request, and the casual bug-report framing ('just turn it off before bed') satirizes tech culture's breezy dismissal of alarming product behavior. Original, dark, and well-executed.

jokes.text: About to get some pennies! Pennies, oh, pennies, oh, pennies.
jokes.setup: Donna is about to go pitch to investors/donors for her commission.
jokes.punchline: Donna's pre-hustle chant is 'pennies, oh, pennies' — an understatement song about money, suggesting either irony about small earnings or just Donna being Donna.
jokes.explanation: A small character moment — Donna's hustle-mode is always funny, but 'pennies' chant is a bit underwritten. It's charming rather than hilarious.

jokes.text: Hello, Ron. I just want you to know that I am not sorry that I pushed you into a giant cake. / Well, I am sorry that I attended a public event.
jokes.setup: Leslie approaches Ron after the candle fight/cake incident.
jokes.punchline: Ron's response to the whole debacle is not to address the cake push, but to be sorry he attended a public event in the first place — pure Ron philosophy.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best line. Ron's regret being about 'attending a public event' rather than anything that happened there is PERFECTLY Ron Swanson — his consistent anti-social philosophy, his hatred of crowds and events, all distilled into one sentence. 'I am sorry that I attended a public event' as a response to being pushed into a cake is sublime. High economy, maximum character integration, highly quotable. This approaches the 8.5 anchor quality.

jokes.text: Yo, Ron. Come on, bud. We're gonna go play some video games, and we want you to watch quietly.
jokes.setup: The Gryzzl tech-bros approach Ron after the gala chaos.
jokes.punchline: They invite Ron to come watch them play video games — specifically to 'watch quietly,' which is simultaneously condescending and oddly appropriate for Ron. Ron presumably just goes with them, without objection.
jokes.explanation: 'Watch quietly' is the perfect qualifier — it implies Ron will be there but participating minimally, which suits him perfectly. The image of Ron silently observing tech bros play video games is inherently funny.

jokes.text: And then we need to sign a suicide pact because our lives are meaningless.
jokes.setup: Ben and April are casually listing errands (renters insurance, grocery store).
jokes.punchline: April inserts 'sign a suicide pact because our lives are meaningless' between mundane errands with total deadpan, treating nihilism as another to-do list item.
jokes.explanation: Pure April — slipping existential nihilism into a domestic to-do list with the same register as 'pick up milk.' The placement between mundane errands is the whole joke, and the delivery (implied total deadpan) makes it. 'Because our lives are meaningless' as an errand qualifier is extremely quotable and highly character-specific.

jokes.text: And then we need to stop by the grocery store. And then we need to sign a suicide pact because our lives are meaningless.
jokes.setup: Andy and April are listing mundane adult errands
jokes.punchline: April inserts 'sign a suicide pact because our lives are meaningless' between 'grocery store' and the next errand
jokes.explanation: An excellent April joke. Structurally, it mimics a mundane errand list — the dark absurdism lands because it's sandwiched between grocery store and presumably more errands. The specificity ('suicide pact' rather than a vaguer complaint) and April's deadpan delivery elevates this above a standard dark joke. Highly quotable and deeply April-coded.

jokes.text: It's the creepy warehouse district. It's mostly just raccoons and old car batteries.
jokes.setup: Andy and April discover they've ended up in an unknown part of Pawnee while looking for the renters insurance office.
jokes.punchline: April's description of the area — 'raccoons and old car batteries' — as the defining features of the neighborhood.
jokes.explanation: A quick, effective establishing joke for the location. 'Old car batteries' alongside raccoons is the specific weird detail that makes it work rather than just saying 'sketchy neighborhood.'

jokes.text: 'I've known a lot of ballers in my day. But no man balls harder than the man I'm about to bring up. He's kind. He's intelligent. He's a person I'm deeply proud to call my friend.'
jokes.setup: Tom reads his prepared speech for Ben, which is genuinely moving.
jokes.punchline: The speech opens with 'I've known a lot of ballers in my day. No man balls harder.' — Tom's earnest attempt at a moving tribute, using 'baller' language for sincere compliment. The vocabulary undermines the formality but the sentiment is real.
jokes.explanation: 'No man balls harder' as a sincere tribute combines Tom's voice with genuine affection — it's funny because of the vocabulary choice but touching because Tom means it. Good character integration and slightly warm-hearted, which gives it rewatch value.

jokes.text: It was a pretty good speech. I mean, it was a little sappy maybe. / [Long pause, Ben is clearly moved] / But I think I liked it.
jokes.setup: Tom has just read his heartfelt speech about their friendship.
jokes.punchline: Ben visibly processes the emotion, initially deflects with 'a little sappy,' then pauses — and the pause is the joke — before admitting 'I think I liked it.' The understatement of 'I think I liked it' about something that clearly moved him.
jokes.explanation: The comedic pause functions as a reaction beat — Ben fighting and losing the battle against being moved. 'I think I liked it' is perfectly calibrated understatement: not 'it was great,' not 'I hated it,' the qualifier 'I think' doing a lot of emotional work. Ben's character (analytical, uncomfortable with sentimentality) is well-served.

jokes.text: Is this a circle? Or is it an O? Is Oprah involved in your bid? It's a zero.
jokes.setup: Leslie presents her bid — a zero, written by hand.
jokes.punchline: Jessica initially can't read the zero and asks if it's an O and if Oprah is involved — an understandable misread that implies Oprah's involvement in bids is not implausible in this world.
jokes.explanation: The Oprah pivot is unexpected and good — it implies Jessica's world is one where Oprah might just bid on things. The quick clarification/correction structure works cleanly.

jokes.text: And not always in a good way, like when your hot fudge pipeline exploded. Oh, boo-hoo! It all ran off into the lake.
jokes.setup: Leslie is making a speech about the Newport family's 200-year history with Pawnee.
jokes.punchline: A hot fudge pipeline is apparently part of Newport family history; it exploded; Jessica's reaction is 'boo-hoo' followed by noting it 'all ran off into the lake' — both defending her ancestors and being completely unbothered.
jokes.explanation: A hot fudge pipeline is exactly the right kind of Pawnee historical absurdism. 'Boo-hoo!' as Jessica's response to an environmental disaster on her family's record is perfect for her character — utterly dismissive of anything that doesn't affect her money. 'It all ran off into the lake' as if this is a mild footnote is a great specific detail.

jokes.text: Well, yes, admittedly, it did make the fish taste delicious, but it was a PR nightmare.
jokes.setup: Jessica has dismissed the hot fudge pipeline explosion.
jokes.punchline: Leslie grudgingly acknowledges a silver lining (delicious fudge fish) before returning to the PR problem — the 'delicious fish' concession is absurd and delivered like a serious debate point.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant follow-through. 'It did make the fish taste delicious' is the unexpected turn — Leslie can't help acknowledging a genuine positive while in the middle of making an argument against. The deadpan 'but it was a PR nightmare' brings it back. Very Leslie: unable to be fully partisan even in a pitch.

jokes.text: It says here there are 12 closets, three bomb shelters, five dumbwaiters, two and three-eighths baths, no kitchens. / It's a fairly standard layout.
jokes.setup: Andy and April are touring a bizarre house for sale.
jokes.punchline: The realtor describes a layout with bomb shelters, dumbwaiters, zero kitchens, and fractional bathrooms as 'fairly standard' — the deadpan normalization of an insane floor plan.
jokes.explanation: The accumulation of bizarre details (bomb shelters, dumbwaiters, no kitchen, 2 and 3/8 baths) is well-paced, and 'fairly standard layout' is the perfect deadpan button. 'Two and three-eighths baths' is a specifically absurd detail — the fraction implies extreme precision about a fraction of a bathroom.

jokes.text: Is that a staircase to nowhere? Yes, it is. Good eye.
jokes.setup: Andy and April are touring the bizarre house.
jokes.punchline: There's a staircase to nowhere; the realtor confirms it and compliments Andy for noticing, treating it as a feature rather than an obvious architectural oddity.
jokes.explanation: 'Good eye' as a response to spotting a staircase to nowhere is the joke — the realtor's real estate enthusiasm treating a bizarre defect as a notable architectural detail worth praising the buyer for identifying.

jokes.text: What was this place? Remember the Pawnee Doll Head Factory? This was a doll head factory? No. This was a holding cell for people who went insane on the assembly line.
jokes.setup: Andy asks about the history of the strange building.
jokes.punchline: The building was not a doll head factory but rather 'a holding cell for people who went insane on the assembly line' — a dark and specific piece of Pawnee lore delivered matter-of-factly.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely dark and original piece of Pawnee world-building. The correction ('No, this was a holding cell for people who went insane') treats industrial-era worker abuse as local color. The specificity of the doll head factory as adjacent lore is beautifully weird. This kind of dark-absurdist Pawnee history joke is some of the show's best material.

jokes.text: What's behind this door? Fire pole! [Enthusiastic discovery]
jokes.setup: They continue exploring the bizarre house.
jokes.punchline: Andy opens a door to find a fire pole — his absolute delight at this discovery reveals that for him, a fire pole is the ultimate house feature.
jokes.explanation: Andy's fire pole enthusiasm is peak Andy — the child in a man's body discovering something exciting in a house of horrors. The one-word punchline ('Fire pole!') with implied delight is economical and character-perfect.

jokes.text: So this place has had zero offers? People seem to be scared off, on account of it being haunted and disgusting.
jokes.setup: Andy has seen the bizarre, dark-history house and asks about offers.
jokes.punchline: The realtor confirms it's haunted and disgusting with complete matter-of-factness, as if these are standard listing disclosures.
jokes.explanation: 'Haunted and disgusting' delivered as real estate disclosure language is the joke. The casual pairing of 'haunted' (paranormal) with 'disgusting' (practical) as co-equal selling obstacles is well-constructed.

jokes.text: After 47 years living here, I decided to move to Orlando to be closer to Disney World. [Previous owner talking head]
jokes.setup: Context for why the house is being sold after a long tenure.
jokes.punchline: The previous owner lived 47 years in a haunted, disgusting holding cell for insane factory workers... and the reason they're leaving is to be closer to Disney World. The casual non-explanation for a baffling choice.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in what ISN'T said — 47 years in this building, and the departure is prompted by wanting Disney World proximity (not the haunting or the insane asylum history). Effective understatement.

jokes.text: We are responsible adults. You know what that means? I know. We have money. And we are going to buy the [expletive] out of this house!
jokes.setup: Andy and April's 'boring adult' arc reaches its resolution in the haunted doll-factory-adjacent building.
jokes.punchline: Their responsible adulthood (having money) is deployed for the most irresponsible possible purchase — a haunted, disgusting former asylum. The reversal completes the episode arc: being an adult means they CAN do crazy things.
jokes.explanation: Strong structural payoff to the episode's Andy/April arc. The irony is perfect: adult responsibility (savings) enables their most irresponsible decision yet. 'We're going to buy the [expletive] out of this house' in April's deadpan is the right tone. This is a satisfying escalation and callback to the whole thread.

jokes.text: I'm Attorney Trevor Nelsson with the law firm Fwar, Dips, Winshares, Gritt, Babip, Pecota, Vorp and Eckstein
jokes.setup: The attorney reads out his law firm name at a press conference.
jokes.punchline: The firm name is a list of sabermetric baseball statistics — WAR, DIPS, Win Shares, GRIT, BABIP, PECOTA, VORP — plus Eckstein (David Eckstein, famous gritty player). A deep baseball analytics joke.
jokes.explanation: A niche-but-brilliant sabermetrics joke hidden in a law firm name. Ben Wyatt's established love of calculus/stats makes this feel earned in the show's universe. BABIP, PECOTA, VORP are obscure enough that only baseball nerds catch all of them — rewatchable because you catch more on repeat. High originality for the specific encoding of the joke. This is the kind of deep-cut joke that rewards attentive viewers.

jokes.text: Well, you did convince three unsuspecting toddlers that peas turn into cupcakes in their tummies.
jokes.setup: Leslie is doubting her ability to convince the Newports that a zero-dollar bid is better than $90 million.
jokes.punchline: Ben's evidence for Leslie's persuasive powers is that she convinced her own toddlers that peas become cupcakes after digestion — an absurd parenting lie deployed as proof of world-class persuasion.
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully specific parenting joke embedded in a motivational speech. 'Three unsuspecting toddlers' is the right framing. The specific lie (peas → cupcakes in the tummy) is inventive and deeply Leslie. Ben using this as a serious argument for Leslie's persuasive gifts is also character-perfect — he's not being ironic, he genuinely considers this impressive.

jokes.text: In the words of Jason Bourne, 'This is where it started for me. This is where it ends.' / You know, I still think Kevin James was a weird choice for the reboot. / Oh, I don't. I think he nailed it.
jokes.setup: Leslie quotes Jason Bourne for motivation; Ben has apparently seen the new Bourne film (which Andy called 'pretty funny' earlier).
jokes.punchline: Ben thinks Kevin James (a comedic actor known for slapstick) was a weird choice for Jason Bourne; Leslie thinks he 'nailed it.' The callback to Andy's earlier description of Bourne as 'pretty funny' pays off here.
jokes.explanation: The callback completes a running joke planted earlier. Kevin James as Jason Bourne is an inspired absurd casting choice for a fictional universe where the franchise apparently went comedy. 'Oh, I don't. I think he nailed it.' from Leslie is a perfect button — she's a Kevin James defender. Rewards attentive viewers who caught Andy's earlier comment.

jokes.text: You know, I still think Kevin James was a weird choice for the reboot. / Oh, I don't. I think he nailed it.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just quoted 'Jason Bourne'
jokes.punchline: The show establishes that in this 2017 version, Kevin James played Jason Bourne in the reboot — Ben finds it weird; Leslie thinks he nailed it
jokes.explanation: A great bit of near-future world-building comedy. Kevin James as Jason Bourne is a perfectly absurd casting choice, and Leslie's earnest defense ('I think he nailed it') is the ideal reaction. The joke rewards the show's 2017 setting premise and is funnier for the specificity of the casting.

jokes.text: Attention! This is war. You guys are going down. And that's all I wanted to say. Except Donna, Tom, hey. I'm sorry I haven't kept in better touch with you recently... So, it's really good to see you both. And also, prepare for war because you chose the wrong side and we are gonna smoke you.
jokes.setup: Leslie comes to confront Tom and Donna who are on the opposing side.
jokes.punchline: Leslie interrupts her war declaration with a genuine, warm apology for not staying in touch — humanizing the conflict — and then immediately returns to war threats. The emotional whiplash is Leslie at her most Leslie.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the most Leslie Knope moments in the episode. She cannot sustain enemy mode without her genuine affection breaking through, and then she pivots BACK to enemy mode. The structure (war → warmth → war) is perfect for her character. 'We are gonna smoke you' after 'it's really good to see you both' is the contradiction that defines her.

jokes.text: And also I made cookies, but Ron is not allowed to eat them and they say 'Prepare for War' on them, but the O in the word 'for' is a heart. And I ate a lot of 'em on the way over here. Because we're at war.
jokes.setup: Leslie continues her war declaration/apology hybrid speech.
jokes.punchline: Three-part joke: (1) war declaration cookies, (2) the O in 'for' is a heart, undermining the war theme, (3) she ate a lot of them on the way there and justifies it as war behavior.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's comedic peak. Three escalating jokes in perfect sequence: Leslie baked themed war cookies (very Leslie), but she couldn't resist making the O a heart (she can't fully commit to hostility), but then she ate most of them pre-delivery (the plan fell apart), and 'Because we're at war' justifies all of it. The self-undermining structure perfectly captures Leslie — she wants to be tough but can't suppress her warmth or her cookie-eating. The heart O is the detail that elevates this to something special. Strongly character-integrated, original structure, and excellent economy.

jokes.text: Also I made cookies, but Ron is not allowed to eat them and they say 'Prepare for War' on them, but the O in the word 'for' is a heart. And I ate a lot of 'em on the way over here.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just declared war on Tom and Donna
jokes.punchline: She brought 'Prepare for War' cookies with a heart in 'for,' banned Ron from eating them, and ate most of them herself en route
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode and possibly one of the best Leslie jokes in the entire series. It works on every level: (1) She made themed cookies for a rivalry confrontation — deeply Leslie. (2) The 'Prepare for War' message with a heart O reveals she cannot help making things loving even in conflict. (3) Ron specifically forbidden from cookies honors their estrangement while also being petty. (4) She ate most of them because she was hungry/anxious/excited — which is the most human and most Leslie detail. Every element is character-specific and earned. The structure builds through three beats, each funnier than the last. The 'heart in for' detail is the standout — it perfectly encapsulates that Leslie Knope literally cannot make something hostile without making it also kind.

jokes.text: Hey, Tom! Hey, man! Buddy, good to see you. How's it going? / It's pretty good. / Hey! Andy! Let's go. / War!
jokes.setup: Leslie is in full war mode; Andy runs into Tom on the way out.
jokes.punchline: Andy and Tom have a completely warm, normal 'good to see you buddy' exchange in the middle of Leslie's war operation, and then Leslie has to snap Andy back with 'War!'
jokes.explanation: A clean reaction beat — Andy's inability to maintain enemy mode because he and Tom are genuinely friends is endearing and funny. 'War!' as the battle cry to snap him out of a friendly chat is a good button.

tmdb_overview: Leslie launches a competition with tech company Gryzzl for a large parcel of land, which she wants to turn into a National Park. April and Andy try to regain their spontaneity. Ben is recognized at a Bicentennial gala, where Tom delivers a speech in his honor.
insight: Seven-year time jump lands 52 jokes in 44 minutes—deadpan understatement carries the reboot.
